title: Why Societies Collapse

paragraphs.text: History warns us that when once-powerful societies collapse, they tend to do so quickly and unexpectedly. But why did these collapses happen? We must expect the answers to be complex, because historical reality is complex: while some societies did indeed collapse spectacularly, others have managed to thrive for thousands of years. When it comes to historical collapses, five groups of interacting factors have been especially important: 1) the damage that people inflict on their environment; 2) climate change; 3) enemies; 4) changes in friendly trading partners; and 5) the society's responses to these changes. That's not to say that all five causes play a significant role in every case; instead, their relative importance varies from case to case. Let's consider some examples stemming from one or more of these causes.

Maya Native Americans of Central America developed the most advanced civilization in the Americas, long before the arrival of Europeans in 1492. They were innovators in writing, astronomy, architecture and art. From local origins around 2,500 years ago, Mayan society reached its peak of population and sophistication in the late 8th century. Thereafter, communities in the most densely populated areas underwent a steep political and cultural collapse. What happened?

A major factor was their farming practices, which brought about deforestation, soil erosion and water management problems, all of which resulted in less food. Those problems were exacerbated by droughts, which may have been partly caused by humans themselves through deforestation. Chronic warfare also made matters worse, as more and more people fought over less and less land and fewer resources. But what of the Mayan kings? Why did they do nothing when they saw their forests vanishing and their hills becoming eroded? Their lack of action could have been because the kings insulated themselves from these troubles by building large fortresses around themselves.

Whereas Mayan societies were undone by problems of their own making, the demise of Polynesian societies on Pitcairn and Henderson Islands in the tropical Pacific Ocean was brought about largely by other people's mistakes. Pitcairn and Henderson Islanders left behind temples as well as the tools used to construct them. The islands are rich in food sources as evidenced by the garbage piles of fish, bird and turtle bones also found. However, the islanders depended on imports from Mangareva Island, hundreds of miles away, for canoes, crops and livestock.

Unfortunately for the inhabitants of Pitcairn and Henderson, their Mangarevan trading partner collapsed for reasons similar to those underlying the Mayan decline: deforestation, erosion and warfare. Deprived of essential imports, the Pitcairn and Henderson societies declined until every body had died or fled.

The Maya and the Henderson and Pitcairn Islanders are not alone, of course. Over the centuries, many other societies have collapsed or died out. Other famous examples include the Anasazi in the American Southwest, who abandoned their cities in the 12th century because of environmental problems and climate change, and the Greenland Norse, who disappeared in the 15th century because of all five interacting factors mentioned earlier. Nevertheless, we should also remember that there is another long list of cultures that have managed to prosper. Societies in Japan, the New Guinea Highlands, and Central and Northwest Europe, for example, have all found ways to sustain themselves. What separates the lost cultures from those that survived?

Half of the answer involves geographical differences. Many of the societies that collapsed had the misfortune to occupy dry, cold or otherwise fragile environments, while many of the long-term survivors enjoyed more robust and fertile surroundings. But a congenial environment does not always guarantee success: some societies (like the Maya) managed to ruin lush environments, while other societies like the Incas, the Inuit, Icelanders and desert Australian Aborigines have managed to carry on in some of the Earth's most daunting environments.

The other half of the answer involves differences in a society's responses to problems. In the 1600s, Japan faced a deforestation crisis, paradoxically brought on by the peace and prosperity following the triumph of the Tokugawa military commanders, or 'shoguns', that ended 150 years of civil war. The subsequent explosion of Japan's population and economy set off rampant logging for construction and fuel. Unlike the Mayan kings, the shoguns responded by turning to fuel-efficient stoves and heaters and to coal in order to reduce wood consumption. At the same time they increased wood production by developing plantation forests. Both the shoguns and the Japanese peasants took a long-term view which motivated them to respond to their problems: the former expected to pass on their power to their children, and the latter expected to pass on their land. Today, despite having the highest human population density of any large developed country, Japan is more than 70 per cent forested.

There is a similar story from Iceland. When the island was first settled by the Norse from Norway, in about AD 870, its light volcanic soils presented the colonists with unfamiliar challenges. Unused to such an environment, they proceeded to cut down trees and stock sheep as if they were still in Norway, with its robust soils. Significant erosion ensued, carrying half of Iceland's topsoil into the ocean within a century or two. Icelanders became the poorest people in Europe. But they gradually learned from their mistakes over time instituting a restriction on sheep stocks and other strict controls.
